title: Phosphocreatine: the first seconds
goal: Explain how phosphocreatine buffers ATP in the first seconds of a sprint, how fast it runs down and recovers, and what that means for repeated efforts and creatine supplements.

steps.title: Creatine kinase: ATP in one step
steps.text:
[PCr](g:pcr) is creatine with a phosphate attached. The enzyme [creatine kinase](g:creatine-kinase) hands that phosphate to ADP in a single step:

**PCr + ADP + H⁺ ⇌ creatine + ATP**

One step means it's the fastest way to rebuild ATP: PCr is the muscle's most immediate ATP reserve [[c:pcr-immediate]]. The moment a sprint starts and ADP rises, the reaction runs to the right and holds ATP almost steady.

Two details matter later:

- It **uses up a proton (H⁺)**, so the start of hard exercise slightly *alkalinises* muscle [[c:ck-proton]].
- It **runs both ways**. In recovery, ATP from the mitochondria pushes it back to the left and rebuilds PCr.

claims.text: PCr is the most immediate reserve for rebuilding ATP at the start of contraction.

evidence.quote: Within the skeletal muscle cell at the onset of muscular contraction, phosphocreatine (PCr) represents the most immediate reserve for the rephosphorylation of adenosine triphosphate (ATP).

claims.text: The creatine kinase reaction consumes a proton, slightly alkalinising muscle at the onset of exercise.

evidence.quote: The proton (H + ) consumption during the creatine kinase reaction accounts for the slight alkalinization of muscle at the onset of exercise.

steps.title: A store that empties in seconds
steps.text:
Resting muscle holds about **80 mmol·kg⁻¹ dry muscle** of PCr: about three times its ATP (25 mmol·kg⁻¹ dry) [[c:pcr-store-size]]. Counting creatine with and without its phosphate, the total pool is about 120 mmol·kg⁻¹ dry, so about two thirds of it is PCr. Some papers use per kg *wet* muscle instead: always check which.

In an all-out effort PCr falls fast [[c:pcr-fast-fall]]:

- after a **6 s** cycle sprint, down by **57%**;
- after a **30 s** sprint, down to about **17–20%** of rest.

So by the last seconds of a 10 s sprint, more than half the store is gone and glycolysis covers much of the ATP.

claims.text: Resting muscle PCr is about 80 and ATP about 25 mmol·kg⁻¹ dry muscle; total creatine averages about 120 mmol·kg⁻¹ dry, about two thirds of it PCr.

evidence.quote: Moreover, at rest, ATP (25 mmol/kg dry weight), ADP (3.3 mmol/kg dry weight), AMP (0.1 mmol/kg dry weight), and PCr (80 mmol/kg dry weight) collectively contain about 70 mmol/kg dry weight of Pi.
About two thirds of intramuscular creatine is phosphocreatine (PCr) with the remaining being free creatine.
The total creatine pool (PCr + Cr) in the muscle averages about 120 mmol/kg of dry muscle mass for a 70 kg individual

claims.text: PCr fell by 57% in a 6 s maximal cycle sprint and to about 17–20% of rest after a 30 s sprint.

evidence.quote: Indeed, within the first 6-s bout of maximal exercise PCr concentration had fallen by 57% and muscle lactate concentration had increased to 28.6 mmol/kg dry wt, confirming significant glycolytic activity.
At the end of sprint 1, PCr was 16.9 +/- 1.4% of the resting value, and muscle pH dropped to 6.69 +/- 0.02.

steps.title: How many seconds of PCr?
steps.problem: Resting muscle holds 80 mmol·kg⁻¹ dry muscle of PCr. Suppose that in a sprint PCr is used at 8 mmol·kg⁻¹ dry·s⁻¹ and nothing else changed. How long until it is empty?
steps: Each PCr rebuilds one ATP, so time = PCr store ÷ rate of PCr use.
In reality the rate of PCr use falls as the store runs down and glycolysis takes a bigger share, so PCr is rarely fully emptied: about 15–20% is left even after exhaustion.

steps.title: Where PCr fits in a maximal effort
steps.text:
The chart splits the energy of maximal efforts lasting 10 s to 4 min into two bands: anaerobic (PCr and glycolysis together) and aerobic.

In words, since the chart can't split the anaerobic band: in the first **5–6 s** the PCr system leads, both in rate and in share of ATP [[c:pcr-dominates]]. Glycolysis starts within seconds and reaches its top rate within about 10–20 s, so by 10 s it is a big partner. The aerobic share is under 10% at 10 s but grows fast: it matches anaerobic supply at about 75–80 s [[c:pcr-crossover]].

A 10 s sprint, a 400 m lap and a 3 km pursuit are three points on one chart, not three separate systems.

diagram.caption: Aerobic vs anaerobic (PCr + glycolysis) share of energy in maximal efforts of 10 s to 4 min.

claims.text: In maximal efforts up to about 5–6 s, the PCr (phosphagen) system dominates the rate and share of ATP resynthesis.

evidence.quote: it has been generally accepted that with an exercise period of maximal effort of up to 5 to 6 seconds duration, the phosphagen energy system dominates in terms of the rate and proportion of total ATP regeneration

claims.text: Aerobic and anaerobic supply are about equal at around 75–80 s of maximal effort.

evidence.quote: The duration of maximal exercise at which equal contributions are derived from the anaerobic and aerobic energy systems appears to occur between 1 to 2 minutes and most probably around 75 seconds
The maximal exercise duration that derived equal contributions from both the anaerobic and aerobic energy systems was 78.6 s (95% confidence interval [95% CI] ± 1.1 s)

steps.title: Rebuilding PCr takes oxygen and minutes
steps.text:
After the effort, creatine kinase runs backwards, using ATP from the mitochondria. That needs oxygen. With blood flow blocked by a cuff, PCr doesn't recover at all [[c:pcr-needs-o2]].

Recovery is roughly exponential: fast, then slower. Its speed is a half-time or a [time constant](g:time-constant) τ (half-time = 0.69 τ):

**fraction of the used PCr rebuilt = 1 − e^(−t/τ)**

Half-times run from about **21 s** for the fast phase after dynamic exercise to about **57 s** after a 30 s all-out sprint, which is τ of about 30–80 s [[c:pcr-half-time]]. Even 6 minutes after a 30 s sprint, PCr was only back to about 85%.

The real curve has a fast and a slow phase; one τ is a simplification.

claims.text: PCr resynthesis depends on oxygen supply: occluding blood flow abolishes it.

evidence.quote: Occlusion of the circulation of the quadriceps completely abolished the resynthesis of PC.

During 15 min incubation in oxygen CP was resynthesized from a starting value of 4% to 68% of the normal value at rest. No resynthesis was observed when parallel muscle samples were incubated for the same time in nitrogen.

claims.text: PCr recovery half-times range from about 21–22 s (fast phase) to about 57 s after a 30 s sprint; PCr reached only about 85% of rest after 6 min.

evidence.quote: The time course of PC resynthesis during recovery was biphasic exhibiting a fast and slow recovery component. The half-time for the fast component was 21-22s
During recovery, PCr increased rapidly to 65.0 +/- 2.8% of rest after 1.5 min, but reached only 85.5 +/- 3.5% of rest after 6 min of recovery.
Modelling of the individual PCr resynthesis using a power function curve gave an average half-time for PCr resynthesis of 56.6 +/- 7.3 s.

steps.title: How much PCr is back after 90 s?
steps.problem: After a 30 s all-out effort, a rider's PCr is at 20% of rest. Take a recovery half-time of 57 s. How much PCr is back after 90 s of easy spinning?
steps: Half-time to time constant: τ = 57 ÷ 0.69 ≈ 82 s.
Fraction of the used PCr rebuilt = 1 − e^(−90/82) = 1 − e^(−1.10) = 1 − 0.33 = 0.67.

PCr now ≈ 20% + 53% = 73% of rest. (Measured in the study: 65% at 90 s. The model is a little optimistic: the study fitted a power curve, not one exponential, and real recovery has a fast and a slow phase.)

steps.title: Repeated sprints, attacks and surges
steps.text:
In a criterium you sprint out of every corner, and every attack you answer is a short all-out effort. How much power you have for the next one tracks how much PCr you have rebuilt [[c:pcr-power-recovery]].

The second effort also leans more on the aerobic route: in a repeated 30 s sprint, aerobic metabolism supplied about half the energy [[c:aerobic-second-sprint]].

Since PCr recovery runs on oxidative ATP, fitter athletes should recover faster. Reviews agree aerobic fitness helps repeated-sprint recovery, but the direct link to PCr recovery rate is inconsistent.

Training point: a short rest (30–60 s) means each rep starts with PCr only partly back; long rests (3–6 min) keep the first seconds of each rep strong.

claims.text: Recovery of sprint power closely tracks PCr resynthesis between repeated sprints.

evidence.quote: High correlations (r = 0.71-0.86; P < 0.05) were found between the percentage resynthesis of PCr and the percentage restoration of PPO, maxSp and MPO6 after 1.5 and 3 min of recovery.
High correlations were found between the percentage of PCr resynthesis and the percentage recovery of power output and pedaling speed during the initial 10 s of sprint 2

claims.text: In a second 30 s sprint after 4 min rest, aerobic metabolism supplied about 49% of the energy.

evidence.quote: These data suggest that aerobic metabolism provides a significant part (approximately 49%) of the energy during the second sprint, whereas PCr availability is important for high power output during the initial 10 s.

debate.question: Does higher aerobic fitness speed up PCr recovery after intense exercise?

sides.position: Yes: aerobic fitness enhances recovery from intermittent high-intensity exercise, partly through faster PCr regeneration, especially with large muscle mass.
Not clearly: the mechanism predicts it, but 31P-MRS studies are inconsistent and limited by method, so the link is unproven.

steps.title: Creatine supplements, briefly
steps.text:
Can you make the PCr store bigger? Yes: creatine monohydrate raises muscle creatine and PCr by about **20–40%**. The quick way is about 0.3 g·kg⁻¹ body mass per day for 5–7 days, then 3–5 g per day [[c:creatine-loading]].

The ISSN position stand finds it improves repeated high-intensity efforts. The one consistent side effect is weight gain: early studies found about 0.5–1 L of extra body water after loading [[c:creatine-effects]]. For a road climber or a runner, that extra mass can cost more than the sprint gains.

The position stand is a consensus statement, but several authors have creatine-industry ties and it was written at the request of a supplement-industry body, so we grade it one step down.

claims.text: Creatine supplementation raises muscle creatine and PCr by 20–40%; loading at about 0.3 g·kg⁻¹·day⁻¹ for 5–7 days then 3–5 g·day⁻¹ is the quickest method.

evidence.quote: Therefore, dietary supplementation of creatine serves to increase muscle creatine and PCr by 20–40%
The quickest method of increasing muscle creatine stores may be to consume ~0.3 g/kg/day of creatine monohydrate for 5–7-days followed by 3–5 g/day thereafter to maintain elevated stores.

claims.text: Creatine loading improves high-intensity and repeated exercise performance; its only consistent side effect is weight gain from fluid retention (about 0.5–1.0 L).

evidence.quote: After creatine loading, performance of high intensity and/or repetitive exercise is generally increased by 10–20% depending on the magnitude of increase in muscle PCr
The only consistently reported side effect from creatine supplementation that has been described in the literature has been weight gain
For example, initial studies reported that creatine loading promoted a short-term fluid retention (e.g., about 0.5 – 1.0 L) that was generally proportional to the acute weight gain observed

points: Creatine kinase rebuilds ATP from PCr in one step (PCr + ADP + H⁺ ⇌ Cr + ATP): the fastest route, and it runs backwards in recovery.
PCr is about 80 mmol·kg⁻¹ dry muscle, three times ATP; it falls by about half in 6 s of all-out work and to about 20% after 30 s.
PCr resynthesis needs oxygen; half-times of about 20–60 s mean it takes minutes to get most of it back.
Power in repeated sprints, attacks and surges tracks PCr recovery; the link with aerobic fitness is plausible but inconsistent.
Creatine loading raises PCr 20–40% and helps repeated hard efforts, at the cost of some weight gain, mostly water.

variants.stem: In the first second of a sprint, what does creatine kinase do?

options.text: Moves a phosphate from PCr to ADP, making ATP
options.why: Right: PCr + ADP + H⁺ → creatine + ATP, in one step.

options.text: Moves a phosphate from ATP to creatine, making PCr
options.why: That is the reverse direction, which happens in recovery, not at the start of a sprint.

options.text: Splits PCr with oxygen to release energy for myosin
options.why: The reaction needs no oxygen, and myosin only uses ATP, never PCr directly.

options.text: Turns creatine into lactate to buffer acid
options.why: Creatine isn't turned into lactate; lactate comes from pyruvate in glycolysis.

variants.stem: During the first seconds of a 100 m sprint, the creatine kinase reaction takes up a proton. What does that do to the muscle?

options.text: Makes it slightly more alkaline at first
options.why: Right: using up H⁺ slightly alkalinises muscle at the onset of exercise.

options.text: Makes it sharply more acidic at once
options.why: Creatine kinase consumes protons; the acid in sprints comes mainly from ATP turnover with glycolysis.

options.text: Stops glycolysis from starting
options.why: Glycolysis starts within seconds regardless; in a 6 s sprint it supplies about half the energy.

options.text: Has no effect on muscle pH
options.why: Consuming H⁺ does raise pH a little; the effect is small but measurable.

variants.stem: Muscle holds 80 mmol·kg⁻¹ dry muscle of PCr. In a sprint finish PCr is used at 6.4 mmol·kg⁻¹ dry·s⁻¹. If the rate stayed constant, how long would PCr last?

options.why: This divides the rate by the store (6.4 ÷ 80). Time = store ÷ rate.
This multiplies store by rate (80 × 6.4); the units don't give seconds.
This adds the ATP store (25 mmol·kg⁻¹ dry) too: (80 + 25) ÷ 6.4. The question asks for one store alone.

variants.solution: Time = store ÷ rate of use = 80 mmol·kg⁻¹ dry ÷ 6.4 mmol·kg⁻¹ dry·s⁻¹ = 12.5 s.

variants.stem: Muscle holds 80 mmol·kg⁻¹ dry muscle of PCr. A track sprinter's standing start uses PCr at 10 mmol·kg⁻¹ dry·s⁻¹. If the rate stayed constant, how long would PCr last?

options.text: 8 s
options.why: Right: 80 ÷ 10 = 8 s.
This divides the rate by the store (10 ÷ 80). Time = store ÷ rate.
This multiplies store by rate (80 × 10); the units don't give seconds.
This adds the ATP store (25 mmol·kg⁻¹ dry) too: (80 + 25) ÷ 10. The question asks for one store alone.

variants.solution: Time = store ÷ rate of use = 80 mmol·kg⁻¹ dry ÷ 10 mmol·kg⁻¹ dry·s⁻¹ = 8 s.

variants.stem: After creatine loading, a rider's PCr rises by 20% to 96 mmol·kg⁻¹ dry muscle. In a sprint PCr is used at 8 mmol·kg⁻¹ dry·s⁻¹. If the rate stayed constant, how long would PCr last?

options.why: Right: 96 ÷ 8 = 12 s, two seconds more than the 10 s from 80 mmol·kg⁻¹ dry.
This uses the normal store (80 ÷ 8) and forgets the 20% rise.
This multiplies store by rate (96 × 8); the units don't give seconds.
This adds the ATP store (25 mmol·kg⁻¹ dry) too: (96 + 25) ÷ 8. The question asks for one store alone.

variants.solution: Time = store ÷ rate of use = 96 mmol·kg⁻¹ dry ÷ 8 mmol·kg⁻¹ dry·s⁻¹ = 12 s.

variants.stem: A track cyclist does a 6 s all-out sprint. What would a muscle biopsy taken right after most likely show for PCr?

options.text: Down by about half
options.why: Right: in a 6 s maximal cycle sprint PCr fell by 57%.

options.text: Down by less than 10%
options.why: PCr is used from the first second at a very high rate; it falls a lot in 6 s.

options.text: Completely used up
options.why: 6 s isn't enough to empty it; even after 30 s, about 17–20% is left.

options.text: Slightly higher than at rest
options.why: PCr only rises in recovery, when ATP from the mitochondria rebuilds it.

variants.stem: A road sprinter launches a 30 s all-out effort from 300 m out. At the line, what is the most likely state of PCr in the leg muscles?

options.text: About a fifth of the resting store left
options.why: Right: after 30 s all-out, PCr is at about 17–20% of rest.

options.text: About half the resting store left
options.why: That fits a 6 s sprint; after 30 s far more has been used.

options.text: Completely used up, zero left
options.why: PCr is rarely emptied completely; about 15–20% remains even at exhaustion.

options.text: Back near rest, rebuilt by glycolysis
options.why: Glycolysis supplies ATP during the sprint, but PCr is rebuilt mainly afterwards, with oxygen.

variants.stem: For a 10 s all-out sprint finish, which statement fits the energy-systems chart best?

options.text: PCr and glycolysis supply most; the aerobic share is small
options.why: Right: at 10 s the two anaerobic routes dominate, but the aerobic route already contributes a little.

options.text: PCr supplies all of it; the others haven't started
options.why: This is the sequential myth: glycolysis is well under way by 10 s and aerobic supply starts at once.

options.text: Glycolysis and the aerobic route supply equal shares
options.why: Aerobic and anaerobic supply only become equal around 75 s.

options.text: The aerobic route supplies most of it
options.why: The aerobic route can't reach a high enough rate in 10 s to supply most of the ATP.

variants.stem: Researchers inflate a cuff around the thigh right after exhausting exercise, so no blood reaches the quadriceps. What happens to PCr while the cuff is on?

options.text: It stays low until the cuff is released
options.why: Right: occlusion completely abolished PCr resynthesis; it only resumed once blood flow returned.

options.text: It recovers normally, since creatine kinase needs no oxygen
options.why: The forward reaction needs no oxygen, but rebuilding PCr needs ATP from the mitochondria, which need oxygen.

options.text: It recovers faster, since glycolysis takes over
options.why: Glycolysis can't rebuild PCr at a useful rate in recovery; resynthesis stopped completely.

options.text: It recovers about halfway, then stalls
options.why: With the cuff on, there was no resynthesis at all, not partial recovery.

variants.stem: Muscle samples taken after a fatiguing contraction are kept for 15 minutes either in oxygen or in nitrogen. What best predicts the result for PCr?

options.text: Rebuilt in oxygen, not rebuilt in nitrogen
options.why: Right: in oxygen PCr went from 4% to 68% of rest; in nitrogen there was no resynthesis.

options.text: Rebuilt equally in both, as it is anaerobic
options.why: PCr breakdown is anaerobic; its resynthesis depends on oxidative ATP.

options.text: Rebuilt only in nitrogen, as oxygen damages it
options.why: Oxygen doesn't damage PCr; it is required to rebuild it.

options.text: Rebuilt in neither, as only blood can rebuild it
options.why: Isolated samples rebuilt PCr in oxygen: what blood brings is oxygen, not a special factor.

variants.stem: PCr recovery has a time constant τ of 30 s. What fraction of the PCr used has been rebuilt after 60 s?

options.why: This is e^(−2): the fraction still missing, not the fraction rebuilt.
This treats τ as a half-time (two half-times = 75%). τ is longer than the half-time.
This assumes linear recovery (60 s is 2 × τ, so done). Exponential recovery never quite reaches 100%.

variants.stem: After a hard 400 m track rep, a runner's PCr recovers with τ = 40 s. What fraction of the PCr used has been rebuilt after 40 s of rest?

options.why: Right: 1 − e^(−1) = 0.63. After one τ, 63% of the gap is closed.
This is e^(−1): the fraction still missing, not the fraction rebuilt.
This treats τ as a half-time. After one half-time 50% is back; after one τ, 63%.
This assumes linear recovery finishing after one τ. Exponential recovery never quite reaches 100%.

variants.stem: In a criterium, a rider's PCr recovers with τ = 25 s. What fraction of the PCr used in one attack has been rebuilt after 75 s?

options.why: This is e^(−3): the fraction still missing, not the fraction rebuilt.
This treats τ as a half-time (three half-times = 87.5%). τ is longer than the half-time.
This assumes linear recovery (75 s is 3 × τ, so done). Exponential recovery never quite reaches 100%.

variants.stem: A study reports a PCr recovery half-time of 21 s. What is the time constant τ?

options.why: Right: τ = half-time ÷ ln 2 = 21 ÷ 0.69 ≈ 30 s.
This multiplies by ln 2 (21 × 0.69) instead of dividing. τ is always longer than the half-time.
This treats τ and half-time as the same; after one τ, 63% is back, not 50%.
This doubles the half-time; the factor is 1/ln 2 ≈ 1.44, not 2.

variants.solution: Half-time = τ × ln 2, so τ = 21 s ÷ 0.693 = 30 s.

variants.stem: After a 30 s all-out sprint, PCr recovery had a half-time of 56 s. What is the time constant τ?

options.why: This multiplies by ln 2 (56 × 0.69) instead of dividing. τ is always longer than the half-time.
This treats τ and half-time as the same; after one τ, 63% is back, not 50%.
This doubles the half-time; the factor is 1/ln 2 ≈ 1.44, not 2.

variants.stem: A 31P-MRS test on a triathlete's calf gives a PCr recovery half-time of 35 s. What is the time constant τ?

options.why: This multiplies by ln 2 (35 × 0.69) instead of dividing. τ is always longer than the half-time.
This treats τ and half-time as the same; after one τ, 63% is back, not 50%.
This doubles the half-time; the factor is 1/ln 2 ≈ 1.44, not 2.

variants.stem: A runner does 8 × 400 m hard with 60 s standing rest. Her heart rate falls well between reps, yet the first 50 m of each rep feel flat. Best explanation?

options.text: PCr is only partly rebuilt after 60 s
options.why: Right: with half-times of about 20–60 s, a minute brings back only part of the PCr, and the first seconds of each rep depend on it.

options.text: Her muscle ATP store is empty
options.why: ATP never runs out: it falls by about a third at most. The limit is how fast it can be rebuilt.

options.text: Lactate left in the muscle blocks contraction
options.why: Power recovery tracked PCr resynthesis, not muscle pH or lactate, in sprint studies.

options.text: Her glycogen ran out after a few reps
options.why: Muscle glycogen lasts far longer than 8 × 400 m; it is not what limits early-rep power.

variants.stem: In a criterium, a rider responds to attacks 30 s apart. Each jump gets weaker, then after a 3-minute lull his jump is nearly back to normal. Best explanation?

options.text: PCr recovery needs minutes, not 30 s
options.why: Right: 30 s rebuilds only part of the PCr; a few minutes brings most of it back.

options.text: His ATP store refills only after 3 minutes
options.why: ATP stays near-constant; it's the PCr buffer behind it that takes minutes to rebuild.

options.text: Lactate must be fully cleared before he can jump
options.why: Power recovery followed PCr, not muscle pH, which stayed low for minutes.

options.text: His muscles had no oxygen during the attacks
options.why: Oxygen delivery continues; what differs is the time available to rebuild PCr.

variants.stem: A forum post claims: "A higher VO₂max always means faster PCr recovery." What is the best judgement on the evidence?

options.text: Plausible, but measured links are inconsistent
options.why: Right: PCr resynthesis runs on oxidative ATP, but 31P-MRS studies relating aerobic power to PCr recovery are inconsistent.

options.text: Proven: every study finds the link
options.why: Reviews report that PCr recovery after single intense bouts doesn't always correlate with VO₂max.

options.text: Wrong: PCr recovery is anaerobic
options.why: PCr breakdown is anaerobic, but its resynthesis needs oxygen: occlusion stops it.

options.text: Wrong: it depends only on muscle pH
options.why: pH mainly governs the slow phase; the fast phase is linked to oxidative ATP supply.

variants.stem: A landmark study in 14 young men (biopsies in 8) found r = 0.71–0.86 between PCr resynthesis and recovery of sprint power. What most limits the claim that PCr recovery causes power recovery in all athletes?

options.text: A small all-male sample and a correlation
options.why: Right: biopsies in only 8 of 14 men limit generalising to women and other groups, and a correlation doesn't prove cause.

options.text: Correlations of 0.7–0.9 are too weak to mean much
options.why: These are high correlations; the problem is sample and design, not the size of r.

options.text: PCr was measured in blood, not in muscle
options.why: PCr was measured in muscle biopsies; it is not a blood marker.

options.text: Cycle ergometers cannot measure sprint power
options.why: Ergometers measure power accurately; this is a misconception about the method.

variants.stem: Which athlete is most likely to gain on balance from creatine loading?

options.text: A track team sprinter doing repeated maximal efforts
options.why: Right: creatine helps repeated high-intensity efforts, and a little extra mass matters less on a flat track.

options.text: A marathon runner racing at steady pace
options.why: Steady aerobic racing relies little on PCr, and ~1 kg of water costs energy on every stride.

options.text: A road climber racing a 40-minute ascent
options.why: A 40-minute climb is aerobic, and extra body mass directly lowers W·kg⁻¹.

options.text: An Ironman triathlete in a steady 9-hour race
options.why: PCr plays almost no role in a 9-hour steady effort; the weight gain is a cost with little gain.
